title: Repeating until done
objectives: Repeat with a `while` loop and make sure it stops.
Trace a loop's counter in a table and find off-by-one errors.

screens.title: Round and round
screens.prose: Line 2 is a new kind of line. After line 3 runs, Python jumps back to line 2 and asks its question again.
screens.question: Python reaches line 2 four times. Fill in `n` each time.

hints.text: On the first arrival, has line 3 run yet?
Line 3 runs once between one arrival at line 2 and the next.
First arrival: `n` is still 0. Each pass through line 3 adds 1, so the arrivals see 0, 1, 2 and 3.

feedback.correct: 0, 1, 2, then 3, when the test turns False.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from `n = 0` and add 1 between one arrival and the next.

byKey.r0c1: On the first arrival line 3 has not run yet, so `n` is still 0.
byKey.r3c1: Three passes through line 3 come before the 4th arrival, so `n` is 3.

explain.text: Each pass through line 3 adds 1, and each arrival at line 2 checks `n < 3`. On the 4th arrival `n` is 3, the check is `False`, and Python moves on to line 4, which prints 3. A block that repeats while its test is `True` is a **`while` loop**.

canvas.caption: Lines 2 and 3 repeat; line 4 runs once, at the end

screens.title: Printing on every pass
screens.prose: Now the `print` is inside the loop, above the line that adds 1.
screens.question: What does the program print?

options.why: You printed after adding 1. Line 3 prints before line 4 adds, so the first value printed is 0.
You ran the block when `n` was 3. `3 < 3` is `False`, so the loop ends before printing 3.
You ran the block once, as `if` would. A `while` loop goes back to line 2 after every pass.

hints.text: What is `n` the first time line 3 runs?
The loop stops at the arrival where `n < 3` is False.
Passes print 0, then 1, then 2. Then `n` is 3, the test is False, and nothing more prints.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace each pass: test, print, add 1.

explain.text: Each pass prints `n`, then adds 1, so the block runs for `n` equal to 0, 1 and 2. A variable like `n`, which changes by a fixed step on every pass, is the loop's **counter**. It starts the loop, steps it on, and its value ends it.

screens.title: Counting down
screens.prose: This counter starts at 10 and falls by 3 on each pass.
screens.question: What does line 4 print?

hints.text: List the values `k` takes: 10, then 7, then ...
The loop only stops when `k > 0` is False at line 2.
`k` goes 10, 7, 4, 1. At 1 the test `1 > 0` is still True, so one more pass gives −2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write down every value of `k`, and stop only when `k > 0` is False.

byKey.last-positive: You stopped at 1. `1 > 0` is still `True`, so the block runs once more and `k` becomes −2.
byKey.zero: `k` never lands on 0: it steps 10, 7, 4, 1, −2. The loop stops when the test fails, not at a target value.
byKey.start: The loop changes `k` before line 4 runs. Line 4 shows the value after the last pass.

explain.text: The values are 10, 7, 4, 1 and then −2. The test only fails once `k` has passed 0, so the loop overshoots. A loop stops when its test is `False`, which need not be at a round number.

screens.title: Two things change
screens.prose: A savings pot starts at £100 and gains £20 a year. The loop counts the years until it reaches £150.
screens.question: Fill in `balance` and `years` after each pass.

hints.text: Each pass runs lines 4 and 5 once. What do they add?
Lines 4 and 5 are the block: one adds £20, the other adds 1 year.
Pass 1 gives 120 and 1, pass 2 gives 140 and 2, pass 3 gives 160 and 3. Then `160 < 150` is False.

feedback.correct: After 3 passes the pot holds £160, and the loop stops.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each pass adds 20 to `balance` and 1 to `years`.

byKey.r2c1: After pass 2 the balance is 140, still below 150, so pass 3 runs and gives 160.

explain.text: After pass 2 the pot holds £140, below £150, so pass 3 runs. After pass 3 it holds £160 and the test fails, so line 6 prints `3 160`. One loop can move several variables; `years` is the counter, and `balance` decides when to stop.

screens.title: One pass too many, or too few
screens.prose:
You want to print the whole numbers 1 to 5, one per line. Four versions fill in the two gaps differently.

```python
n = START
while TEST:
    print(n)
    n = n + 1
```
screens.question: Which version prints exactly 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?

options.why: You stopped at `n < 5`. When `n` reaches 5 the test is `False`, so 5 never prints.
You started the counter at 0, so 0 prints first: six numbers.
This prints 0 to 4: it starts one too low and stops one too early.

hints.text: Check each version's first and last printed number.
The first number printed is the start. The last is the largest `n` that still passes the test.
You need the start to be 1 and the last passing value to be 5. `n <= 5` lets 5 through; `n < 5` does not.

feedback.correct: Start at 1, and let 5 pass the test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check both ends: the first value printed and the last.

byKey.lt: You stopped at `n < 5`. When `n` is 5 the test is `False`, so the loop prints only 1 to 4.
byKey.zero-le: Starting at 0 prints 0 as well: six numbers, one too many.

explain.text: Check the two ends: the start is the first number printed, and the last is the largest `n` that passes the test. Getting one end wrong by one is an **off-by-one** error, the commonest loop bug. `n < 6` would also work: it is the same test as `n <= 5` for whole numbers.

screens.title: A loop that never ends
screens.question: What happens when you run it?

options.text: It prints 1 again and again, and never reaches line 4.

options.why: You expected `n` to grow by itself. No line in the block changes `n`, so `n <= 5` stays `True`.
You treated `while` like `if`. After the block, Python goes back to line 2, and the test is still `True`.

options.text: Python stops with an error before printing.
options.why: Every line here is valid Python. The problem only shows when it runs: the test never becomes `False`.

hints.text: Which line changes `n`?
The block is line 3 only.
Nothing in the block changes `n`, so it stays 1 and `n <= 5` is True on every arrival.

feedback.correct: Nothing changes `n`, so the test never fails.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the line that moves `n` towards a False test.

explain.text: Nothing in the block changes `n`, so `n <= 5` is `True` for ever. This is an **infinite loop**. Every `while` loop needs a line in its block that moves it towards a `False` test; in the exercises, tests stop after 5 seconds and say so.

canvas.caption: Line 3 runs for ever; line 4 is never reached

screens.title: How many steps
screens.prose: Write the loop from the savings pot yourself. Start from `start` and add `step` until the value is at least `target`. Return how many additions that took.
screens.question: Write the `while` loop inside `steps_to_reach`.

widget.starter:
def steps_to_reach(start, target, step):
    value = start
    count = 0
    # add step to value until it is at least target,
    # adding 1 to count each time
    
    return count
widget.solution:
def steps_to_reach(start, target, step):
    value = start
    count = 0
    while value < target:
        value = value + step
        count = count + 1
    return count
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, each with a start, a target and a positive step. A start already at the target needs 0 steps.

hints.text: The loop should keep going while the value is still below the target.
The block needs two lines: one moves `value` on, one adds 1 to `count`.
Write `while value < target:`, then indented under it `value = value + step` and `count = count + 1`.

feedback.correct: All six tests passed, including the start that needs no steps.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check a start equal to the target: the loop should run 0 times.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error or ran too long. Check that the block changes `value`, so the test can fail.

explain.text:
The test sits at the top, so a start already at the target skips the block and returns 0. Reaching the target exactly, as 0 to 1000 in steps of 250 does, stops the loop because `1000 < 1000` is `False`.

```python
def steps_to_reach(start, target, step):
    value = start
    count = 0
    while value < target:
        value = value + step
        count = count + 1
    return count
```

screens.title: Three things to check
screens.prose:
You traced the same cycle each time: test, block, back to the test. A counter from $a$ in steps of $s$ under `while n < b:` makes $\lceil (b - a)/s \rceil$ passes ($\lceil\cdot\rceil$ rounds up).

```python
count = 0                # 1. where it starts
while count < 3:         # 2. last True value?
    print(count)
    count = count + 1    # 3. moves towards False
```
screens.question: A loop starts with `n = 2`, tests `while n < 10:`, and adds 2 each pass. How many passes?

options.why: You let 10 through. `10 < 10` is `False`, so the block runs for 2, 4, 6 and 8 only.
You counted every number from 2 to 9. The counter jumps by 2 each pass.
You skipped the first pass. The block runs with `n` equal to 2 before any adding.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the values of `n` that pass the test.

explain.text: The block runs with `n` equal to 2, 4, 6 and 8, then `10 < 10` fails. The formula agrees: $\lceil (10 - 2)/2 \rceil = 4$. When in doubt, list the passes by hand.

screens.title: Compounding, pass by pass
screens.prose:
£1,000.00 earns 7% a year, added once a year. This loop counts the years until the balance doubles.

```python
balance = 1000.00
years = 0
while balance < 2000.00:
    balance = balance * 1.07
    years = years + 1
```
screens.question: Fill in `balance`, to the penny, and `years` after each of the first three passes.

hints.text: Each pass multiplies the balance by 1.07.
Pass 2 multiplies the new balance, £1,070.00, not the original £1,000.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the latest balance by 1.07 on each pass.

byKey.r1c1: You added £70 again. The second year's 7% is on £1,070.00, so it adds £74.90.

explain.text: Each pass multiplies the latest balance, so the yearly gain grows: £70.00, then £74.90, then £80.14. That growth is why the balance doubles in 11 years, not the $1/0.07 \approx 14.3$ that simple interest would need.

screens.title: When does it double?
screens.prose: Now let the loop do every year. Given a starting balance and a yearly rate as a decimal, return the whole number of years until the balance is at least double.
screens.question: Complete `years_to_double`.

widget.starter:
def years_to_double(balance, rate):
    target = 2 * balance
    years = 0
    # grow balance by rate once a year
    # until it reaches target
    
    return years
widget.solution:
def years_to_double(balance, rate):
    target = 2 * balance
    years = 0
    while balance < target:
        balance = balance * (1 + rate)
        years = years + 1
    return years
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. `rate` is a decimal, so 7% is `0.07`. A balance that lands exactly on double counts as doubled.

hints.text: Keep going while the balance is still below `target`.
Each year: multiply `balance` by `1 + rate`, then add 1 to `years`.
Write `while balance < target:`, then indented `balance = balance * (1 + rate)` and `years = years + 1`.

feedback.correct: All six tests passed. At 7% the balance doubles in 11 years.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Try a rate of 1.0 by hand: the balance doubles in exactly 1 year.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error or ran too long. Check that the block changes `balance`.

explain.text:
The loop multiplies by $1 + r$ each year and stops at the first year the balance reaches the target. At 7%, $1.07^{10} \approx 1.967$ and $1.07^{11} \approx 2.105$, so it takes 11 years. Traders' rule of 72 guesses $72 / 7 \approx 10.3$, the same ballpark.

```python
def years_to_double(balance, rate):
    target = 2 * balance
    years = 0
    while balance < target:
        balance = balance * (1 + rate)
        years = years + 1
    return years
```

ideas: A `while` loop asks its test, runs its block if `True`, then goes back and asks again.
Check three things: where the counter starts, the last value that passes the test, and the line that moves it on.
A block that never moves the counter towards a `False` test gives an infinite loop; a test that is `False` at once gives zero passes.

formula.name: Passes of a counting loop
formula.note: From $a$ in steps of $s > 0$ under `while n < b:`, when $a < b$; zero passes when $a \ge b$.

summary.trap: `while n < 5` stops before 5. Check both ends of every loop: off-by-one is the commonest loop bug.

quiz.prose:
```python
cash = 50.00
while cash > 100.00:
    cash = cash - 10.00
print(cash)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected the loop to run until the test fails. It fails on the first arrival, so the block never runs.
You ran the block once, as if the test came at the end. It comes first, and `50.0 > 100.0` is `False`.
This loop never starts, so it cannot run for ever.

feedback.correct: The test fails at once, so the block runs zero times.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the test on the very first arrival.

explain.text: `50.0 > 100.0` is `False` on the first arrival, so the block is skipped entirely. A `while` loop can run zero times. Python prints the float as `50.0`.

quiz.prose:
```python
i = 3
while i < 15:
    print(i)
    i = i + 4
```
quiz.question: How many numbers does it print?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the values of `i` that pass the test.

byKey.fifteen: You counted 15. `15 < 15` is `False`, so 15 is never printed.

explain.text: `i` takes 3, 7 and 11, each passing `i < 15`. The next value, 15, fails the test, so three numbers print.

quiz.prose: Each loop starts with `x = 10` and has one line in its block.
quiz.question: Which loop never ends?

options.why: This counts down to 0, and `0 > 0` is `False`, so it ends.
This counts up to 100 and stops there.
Doubling reaches 1280 after seven passes, which fails the test.

feedback.correct: Adding 1 moves `x` away from a False test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each loop, ask whether the block moves `x` towards a False test.

explain.text: With `x > 0` as the test, `x` must fall for the loop to end. Adding 1 moves it the wrong way, so the test stays `True` for ever.

quiz.prose: £1,000.00 grows by 10% a year. A loop counts the years until the balance is at least £1,500.00.
quiz.question: How many years does it count?

feedback.correct: After 4 years it is £1,464.10, still short; year 5 gives £1,610.51.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.1 each year and stop at the first balance of £1,500.00 or more.

byKey.four: After 4 years the balance is £1,464.10, still below £1,500.00, so the loop runs a 5th time.

explain.text: The balances run £1,100.00, £1,210.00, £1,331.00, £1,464.10 and £1,610.51. The first one at or above £1,500.00 is year 5.
